units.translation: Middle form καταξιόομαι [I deem worthy] I deem worthy, I judge worthy
Thus it is customary to say χαίρειν κελεύω [I bid farewell] or λέγω [I say].
and bid many farewells to misfortunes
Justice looked upon him and deemed him worthy
to make cease, to put an end to
to make cease, to put an end to
For who could have stopped the treacherous diseases of Hera?
The big one quickly swallows down the half-opa and the smaller one
he fell at our hands, he died

where Aldus has καταπνείει [breathes upon], M has καταπνέει [breathes upon], but one letter before ει has been erased, which seems to have been υ: hence καταπνεύει [breathes upon] in the copies. Aeschylus perhaps wrote καταπνεῖ μου [breathes upon me].
For still from the gods a persuasion breathes upon the strength of songs, an inborn life-force
Euripides uses this adjective at Or. 178.
And near are the three winged sisters of these

Which is the participle of the second aorist. Hesychius explains καταπλακών [having crouched] by διαμαρτών [having failed], but with another interpretation preceding, καταπλήξας [having struck with fear], perhaps from καταπτήξας [having crouched], which Lobeck conjectured in Paralip. p. 451, corrupted and to be referred to the Aeschylean καταπτακών [having crouched].
This man here is somewhere, having crouched down
having sewn up a fate for Pentheus like a hare

which the scholiast explains as καλῶς ἐν ἡλίῳ γεγυμνασμένους [well exercised in the sun]. Wellauer conjectured κατερρινωμένους [filed down], which verb Hesychius noted as κατερρινωμένον: καταπεπυκασμένον, καταδεδερματωμένον [filed down: thickened, hardened like leather]. If κατερρινημένους [filed down] is correctly read, it must be explained as Paley explained it: "the metaphor conveys the idea of rubbing away and removing all superfluous flesh." Bothe compares Quintil. Or. 8, 3, 12. quorum lacertos exercitatio expressit ac constrinxit. So also Tac. Germ. 30 strictos artus. Lucret. 3, 214 nil ibi limatum de toto corpore cernas.
And they will find many in the midday heat (thus Schuetzius for μεσημβρίαι, i.e. μεσημβρίᾳ, which is in M) with their arms well filed down
well exercised in the sun, filed down
filed down: thickened, hardened like leather, filed down
whether the people's anarchy might cast down the council
Perfect κατήρτυκα [I have matured] intransitively, I have reached full age, i.e. I am adult

Correctly the scholiast: τέλειος τὴν ἡλικίαν [perfect in age]; this is from animals. Hesychius: κατηρτυκώς: τέλειος [having matured: perfect]. Properly of irrational animals, when it has shed all its teeth. More on this use of the verb see in Thes. vol. 4 p. 1214.
